sources.title: M. Dashti and A. M. Stuart, The Bayesian Approach to Inverse Problems (full lecture notes, arXiv:1302.6989v4)
sources.locator: §4.1 Assumptions 4.2, Theorems 4.3 and 4.5 (PDF pp. 36–39); §4.2 Assumptions 4.7, Theorems 4.8 and 4.9 (PDF pp. 40–43); §4.1 Remark 4.6 (PDF p. 39); §7.2.4 Definition 7.11 Hellinger normalization (PDF p. 85).

contents.name: Assumptions 4.2: common lower envelope and data-Lipschitz potential bound
contents.reason: These are the precise data-ball hypotheses retained in the local theorem; the weighted envelope is used to make both square-root and normalizer bounds integrable.

contents.name: Theorem 4.3: evidence propriety under a common lower envelope
contents.reason: The IP-17 statement includes pointwise finite positive evidence, but its proof supplies the support-point neighborhood locally instead of importing the source’s invalid bounded-noncompact-set supremum inference.

contents.name: Theorem 4.5: data-to-posterior Lipschitz continuity in Hellinger distance
contents.reason: This is the principal source claim for the first planned theorem; the local proof rederives the constants in the library root-L2 convention.

contents.name: Assumptions 4.7: shared lower envelope and potential approximation error
contents.reason: These hypotheses are retained with the stated weighted integrability; the local proof obtains large-N normalizer lower bounds from the IP-16 theorem and perturbation.

contents.name: Theorem 4.8: evidence propriety for a potential and its approximation
contents.reason: The discretization statement includes positive finite evidence; its local proof uses the ready IP-16 propriety theorem and an explicit normalizer perturbation bound.

contents.name: Theorem 4.9: potential-approximation Hellinger rate
contents.reason: The statement and weighted envelope match the IP-17 design; the local proof replaces the printed bounded-noncompact-set positivity shortcut.

contents.name: Remark 4.6: Hellinger distance controls expectations under second-moment hypotheses
contents.reason: The finite B-page example illustrates why mean information alone does not determine full-law Hellinger agreement; it does not import the source’s moment inequality.

contents.name: Definition 7.11: source Hellinger normalization
contents.reason: The source includes a factor 1/sqrt(2); the theorem uses the library root-L2 convention and proves its constant directly.

sources.title: J. Latz, On the Well-posedness of Bayesian Inverse Problems, SIAM/ASA Journal on Uncertainty Quantification 8 (2020), arXiv:1902.10257v4
sources.locator: §2.1 Hellinger normalization (PDF p. 6); §3.1 Example 3.1 (PDF pp. 7–8); §3.4 Assumptions 3.5, Theorem 3.6, Lemma 3.7 and its full proof (PDF pp. 10–12 and 24–25).

contents.name: Section 2.1: Hellinger distance normalization
contents.reason: The source uses one half times the root-L2 square; the IP-17 theorem uses the library convention and recomputes the estimate.

contents.name: Example 3.1: a nonlinear data transformation retains continuity but breaks local Lipschitz stability
contents.reason: The example supports retaining the explicit data-Lipschitz potential hypothesis and is not generalized beyond its stated transformed Gaussian model.

contents.name: Assumptions 3.5 and Theorem 3.6: Hellinger continuity under likelihood domination
contents.reason: The stronger local Lipschitz theorem implies continuity on each bounded data ball; the source supplies an independent continuity treatment with different likelihood hypotheses.

contents.name: Lemma 3.7 and proof: posterior continuity in Hellinger distance
contents.reason: The theorem includes this qualitative consequence while proving a stronger linear modulus from the IP-17 weighted potential assumptions.

sources.title: S. L. Cotter, M. Dashti, and A. M. Stuart, Approximation of Bayesian Inverse Problems for PDEs, arXiv:0909.2126v1
sources.locator: §2 Theorem 2.4 and proof (PDF pp. 7–8); Theorem 2.6 and proof (PDF pp. 9–10); Appendix A Definition A.2 and Lemma A.3 (PDF pp. 33–34).

contents.name: Theorem 2.4: linear Hellinger rate under Gaussian exponential-envelope assumptions
contents.reason: The local theorem includes this Gaussian-special-case rate under its hypotheses and proves the more general weighted-envelope estimate directly.

contents.name: Theorem 2.6: Hellinger convergence from compact-set error and Gaussian tail control without a stated linear rate
contents.reason: The B-page counterexample only disproves a universal linear rate under a nonintegrable envelope; it makes no convergence claim for the full sequence and imports none of the source’s separate Gaussian tail assumptions.

contents.name: Definition A.2: source Hellinger normalization
contents.reason: The source uses one half times the root-L2 square; the theorem explicitly uses the library root-L2 convention and rederives its constants.

contents.name: Lemma A.3: Hellinger-to-expectation control under moment assumptions
contents.reason: No source moment inequality is imported; the finite mean counterexample addresses a converse question with an explicit root-L2 calculation.
